On 11 February 2025 the City Council adopted Resolution No. NS-30,438, affirming the City of Santa Cruz commitment to abide by the California Values Act and reaffirming prior Council action restricting the use of City resources for immigration enforcement, together with a direction to the City Manager to work with other local government and non-profit partners committed to that Act. It was taken on the Consent Agenda, the motion carried unanimously, and this member is named in the AYES. That is chair 3 — follow federal law as required but do not use local resources for proactive immigration enforcement — which is what the California Values Act does and what this resolution commits the City to continue doing. It is NOT chair 1: chair 1 turns on refusing all ICE detainers and prohibiting local employees from sharing immigration status information with federal agencies, and neither this resolution nor anything else in the 83 City Council meetings harvested from 10 January 2023 to 13 October 2026 mentions detainers at all, so there is no evidence for the stronger rung. It is not chair 4 or 5, which would have the City offering its resources and information to federal agencies rather than restricting them.

The City Council does set a wage floor and does index it automatically: Ordinance No. 2023-03, adopted 28 February 2023, amended Chapter 5.10 of the Municipal Code so that the living wage is adjusted each year by the Consumer Price Index, and the Council has prescribed the rate by resolution every year since, most recently for fiscal year 2027. That is deliberately NOT seated as chair 1. Section 5.10.060 of the chapter states that the living wage requirement applies to all contracts for services and related subcontracts, so it binds the City as a purchaser of services and the social service agencies it funds, not employers in the city generally. This ladder asks what approach government should take to the minimum wage, and its rungs describe a general wage floor, down to removing it entirely and letting employers and workers set pay by agreement. A procurement standard does not choose among those rungs, so the row stays blank.

On 10 June 2025 the Council adopted Resolution No. NS-30,505 confirming the City commitment to prohibiting offshore drilling in the marine sanctuary off its coast, and directed the Mayor to send a letter opposing the proposed 11th National Outer Continental Shelf Oil and Gas Leasing Program. That is a clear direction but it is not a rung on this ladder, which asks what role fossil fuels should play in the nation energy future and whose rungs run from phasing out production entirely to maximising it and opening more public land and waters. Opposing one federal leasing programme in the waters off this city is a place-specific objection that is consistent with more than one of those national rungs, so the row stays blank rather than being seated at chair 2 on a vote that does not reach it.

On 11 February 2025 the City Council adopted Resolution No. NS-30,438, affirming the City of Santa Cruz commitment to abide by the California Values Act and reaffirming prior Council action restricting the use of City resources for immigration enforcement, together with a direction to the City Manager to work with other local government and non-profit partners committed to that Act. It was taken on the Consent Agenda, the motion carried unanimously, and this member is named in the AYES. That is chair 3 — follow federal law as required but do not use local resources for proactive immigration enforcement — which is what the California Values Act does and what this resolution commits the City to continue doing. It is NOT chair 1: chair 1 turns on refusing all ICE detainers and prohibiting local employees from sharing immigration status information with federal agencies, and neither this resolution nor anything else in the 83 City Council meetings harvested from 10 January 2023 to 13 October 2026 mentions detainers at all, so there is no evidence for the stronger rung. It is not chair 4 or 5, which would have the City offering its resources and information to federal agencies rather than restricting them.

The City Council does set a wage floor and does index it automatically: Ordinance No. 2023-03, adopted 28 February 2023, amended Chapter 5.10 of the Municipal Code so that the living wage is adjusted each year by the Consumer Price Index, and the Council has prescribed the rate by resolution every year since, most recently for fiscal year 2027. That is deliberately NOT seated as chair 1. Section 5.10.060 of the chapter states that the living wage requirement applies to all contracts for services and related subcontracts, so it binds the City as a purchaser of services and the social service agencies it funds, not employers in the city generally. This ladder asks what approach government should take to the minimum wage, and its rungs describe a general wage floor, down to removing it entirely and letting employers and workers set pay by agreement. It was taken on the Consent Public Hearing Agenda, the motion carried unanimously, and this member is named in the AYES. That is chair 2 — strengthen existing rent stabilisation and extend coverage to more units — and the instrument does both halves: the chapter it amends already sets just-cause protection above the state AB 1482 floor, and the amendment carries the rent-increase cap across to a further class of units that would otherwise lose it when their affordability restrictions lapsed. It is NOT chair 1, which requires rent control covering all rental units communitywide; this reaches one defined category of units. It is not chair 3, which would mean keeping current protections as they are rather than extending them to units that did not have them.

On 11 February 2025 the City Council adopted Resolution No. NS-30,438, affirming the City of Santa Cruz commitment to abide by the California Values Act and reaffirming prior Council action restricting the use of City resources for immigration enforcement, together with a direction to the City Manager to work with other local government and non-profit partners committed to that Act. It was taken on the Consent Agenda, the motion carried unanimously, and this member is named in the AYES. That is chair 3 — follow federal law as required but do not use local resources for proactive immigration enforcement — which is what the California Values Act does and what this resolution commits the City to continue doing. It is NOT chair 1: chair 1 turns on refusing all ICE detainers and prohibiting local employees from sharing immigration status information with federal agencies, and neither this resolution nor anything else in the 83 City Council meetings harvested from 10 January 2023 to 13 October 2026 mentions detainers at all, so there is no evidence for the stronger rung. It is not chair 4 or 5, which would have the City offering its resources and information to federal agencies rather than restricting them.

The City Council does set a wage floor and does index it automatically: Ordinance No. 2023-03, adopted 28 February 2023, amended Chapter 5.10 of the Municipal Code so that the living wage is adjusted each year by the Consumer Price Index, and the Council has prescribed the rate by resolution every year since, most recently for fiscal year 2027. That is deliberately NOT seated as chair 1. Section 5.10.060 of the chapter states that the living wage requirement applies to all contracts for services and related subcontracts, so it binds the City as a purchaser of services and the social service agencies it funds, not employers in the city generally. This ladder asks what approach government should take to the minimum wage, and its rungs describe a general wage floor, down to removing it entirely and letting employers and workers set pay by agreement. A procurement standard does not choose among those rungs, so the row stays blank.

On 10 June 2025 the Council adopted Resolution No. NS-30,505 confirming the City commitment to prohibiting offshore drilling in the marine sanctuary off its coast, and directed the Mayor to send a letter opposing the proposed 11th National Outer Continental Shelf Oil and Gas Leasing Program. That is a clear direction but it is not a rung on this ladder, which asks what role fossil fuels should play in the nation energy future and whose rungs run from phasing out production entirely to maximising it and opening more public land and waters. Opposing one federal leasing programme in the waters off this city is a place-specific objection that is consistent with more than one of those national rungs, so the row stays blank rather than being seated at chair 2 on a vote that does not reach it.

On 24 September 2024 the City Council adopted Ordinance No. 2024-16, amending Chapter 21.07 of the Santa Cruz Municipal Code, Just Cause Eviction Above AB 1482 Requirements, to extend AB 1482 rental increase protections to tenants in units with expiring affordable housing rental restrictions. It was taken on the Consent Public Hearing Agenda, the motion carried unanimously, and this member is named in the AYES. That is chair 2 — strengthen existing rent stabilisation and extend coverage to more units — and the instrument does both halves: the chapter it amends already sets just-cause protection above the state AB 1482 floor, and the amendment carries the rent-increase cap across to a further class of units that would otherwise lose it when their affordability restrictions lapsed. It is NOT chair 1, which requires rent control covering all rental units communitywide; this reaches one defined category of units. It is not chair 3, which would mean keeping current protections as they are rather than extending them to units that did not have them.
